question: A policy officer must work through a 180-page regulatory guidance document that is too long to handle usefully in one request. How should she divide it up?
options: A) Into the first fifty pages and the last fifty pages, on the basis that the middle is likely to be mostly detail.
B) Into as many small pieces as possible, so that each request stays short and every piece is handled thoroughly.
C) Into equal blocks of thirty pages each, so that every part of the work is the same size and easy to plan around.
D) Into the document's own chapters, so each part covers one complete topic and can be understood on its own terms.
correct_answers: D) Into the document's own chapters, so each part covers one complete topic and can be understood on its own terms.
explanations: Deciding in advance that the middle is unimportant discards material she has not read, and guidance documents commonly place the operative detail there.
Very small pieces multiply the number of merges and make it more likely that a rule is read without the qualification that governs it.
Fixed page blocks cut through the middle of arguments and definitions, so a part often contains a rule whose scope was set on the previous page.

Correct. The document's own structure marks where topics begin and end, so each part arrives complete, carries its own definitions, and can be summarised without depending on material that was cut away.
